title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays — binary search partition, O(log min(m,n)).
shortTitle: Median of Two Sorted Arrays — Binary Search Partition, O(log min(m,n))

s1_definition.profdef: The Median of Two Sorted Arrays problem finds the median of the combined sorted order of two already-sorted arrays without merging them. The optimal solution binary-searches a partition point in the smaller array, deriving the matching partition in the larger array so that the left side holds exactly half the total elements, then checks that the largest left element does not exceed the smallest right element. It runs in logarithmic time in the size of the smaller array with constant extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has two sorted lists of transaction amounts, Rajesh's and Priya's, and an analyst needs the median amount of both combined without physically merging them. Imagine drawing a vertical cut through each list so that everything to the left of both cuts is the smaller half and everything to the right is the larger half. The analyst slides the cut in the smaller list, computing the matching cut in the larger list, until the two halves balance perfectly, and reads the median off the boundary.
s1_definition.oneliner: Binary-search a partition in the smaller array so left holds half the total and the boundary values cross correctly.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Median of Two Sorted Arrays problem finds the median of the combined sorted order of two already-sorted arrays without merging them. The optimal solution binary-searches a partition point in the smaller array, deriving the matching partition in the larger array so that the left side holds exactly half the total elements, then checks that the largest left element does not exceed the smallest right element. It runs in logarithmic time in the size of the smaller array with constant extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has two sorted lists of transaction amounts, Rajesh's and Priya's, and an analyst needs the median amount of both combined without physically merging them. Imagine drawing a vertical cut through each list so that everything to the left of both cuts is the smaller half and everything to the right is the larger half. The analyst slides the cut in the smaller list, computing the matching cut in the larger list, until the two halves balance perfectly, and reads the median off the boundary.

**One line to remember:** Binary-search a partition in the smaller array so left holds half the total and the boundary values cross correctly.

sections.s2_technical:
The simple approach merges both arrays and reads the middle, which is linear time. The optimal approach gets logarithmic time by never merging. The idea is a partition: pick a cut in the first array that puts some number of its elements on the left, then the matching cut in the second array is forced, because the left side must contain exactly half of the total elements. So if you know how many you took from the first array, you compute how many must come from the second.

You always binary-search on the smaller array to keep the logarithmic factor minimal. Let the smaller array be A with size m and the larger be B with size n. You search for a cut index i in A, from zero to m, and the matching cut in B is j equal to the half-total minus i. The left half consists of the first i elements of A and the first j elements of B. For this partition to be the correct median split, the largest element on the left of A must be less than or equal to the smallest element on the right of B, and symmetrically the largest on the left of B must be less than or equal to the smallest on the right of A.

If the largest left element of A is greater than the smallest right element of B, you took too many from A, so you move the cut in A left. If the largest left element of B is greater than the smallest right element of A, you took too few from A, so you move the cut right. When both crossing conditions hold, you have found the partition. For an even total the median is the average of the maximum of the two left boundaries and the minimum of the two right boundaries; for an odd total it is the maximum of the two left boundaries.

A senior point is the boundary sentinels. When a cut lands at the very start or end of an array, there is no element on one side, so you treat the missing left boundary as negative infinity and the missing right boundary as positive infinity. This lets the crossing comparisons work uniformly without special-casing empty sides, which is where many implementations get subtle bugs.

Another senior point is always searching the smaller array. If you searched the larger one, the computed cut in the smaller could go out of its bounds, and the complexity would be logarithmic in the larger size. Swapping so A is the smaller array guarantees valid cuts and the tightest bound. For money I use BigDecimal for the boundary comparisons and the averaging with a defined rounding mode so the median is exact.

A small finance-domain example: with A as the smaller array, `int i = (lo+hi)/2; int j = half - i;` and checking `A[i-1] <= B[j]` and `B[j-1] <= A[i]` locates the median partition in logarithmic steps.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India keeps two separately sorted lists of transaction amounts, one for Rajesh and one for Priya, and a reporting feature needs the median of both combined to describe the typical transaction size, but the lists are huge and merging them each time is too slow. Finding the median of two sorted arrays by partition binary search is exactly this.

This is exactly how Median of Two Sorted Arrays works in Java — binary-searching a cut in the smaller list and deriving the matching cut in the larger so the halves balance.

Problem 2 — The combined count can be even or odd, needing an average of two boundary values or a single one, and a cut can land at an array edge needing infinity sentinels, and all amounts are exact BigDecimal. This shows the even-odd handling, the edge sentinels, and money precision.

What the code will do: a `MedianFinder` with `medianOfTwo(BigDecimal[] a, BigDecimal[] b)` that searches the smaller array for the balancing partition. The demo computes the median of Rajesh's and Priya's amount lists.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's list is `1000, 3000` and Priya's is `2000`, so the combined order would be `1000, 2000, 3000`.

Step 1: Priya's list is smaller, so we swap to make A the array `2000` with size one and B the array `1000, 3000` with size two. The total is three, so the left half size is two.

Step 2: lo is zero, hi is one. The cut i in A is the midpoint, zero. Then the forced cut j in B is the half-total two minus zero, which is two. The left boundary of A is negative infinity since i is zero, the right boundary of A is `2000`. The left boundary of B is the element before index two, `3000`, and the right boundary of B is positive infinity since j equals n.

Step 3: we check the crossing. Is the A left boundary, negative infinity, less than or equal to the B right boundary, positive infinity? Yes. Is the B left boundary `3000` less than or equal to the A right boundary `2000`? No. So we took too few from A relative to B, meaning the cut in A must move right, so lo becomes one.

Step 4: lo is one, hi is one. The cut i in A is one, so j is two minus one, which is one. The A left boundary is `2000`, the A right boundary is positive infinity since i equals m. The B left boundary is the element at index zero, `1000`, and the B right boundary is the element at index one, `3000`.

Step 5: we check the crossing. Is `2000` less than or equal to `3000`? Yes. Is `1000` less than or equal to positive infinity? Yes. Both hold, so this partition is correct. The total is odd, so the median is the maximum of the two left boundaries, the maximum of `2000` and `1000`, which is `2000`. The even demo balances similarly and averages `2000` and `3000` to `2500.00`.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T19:40:00Z INFO Median = 2000
2026-10-26T19:40:00Z INFO Odd median = 2000
2026-10-26T19:40:00Z INFO Median = 2500.00
2026-10-26T19:40:00Z INFO Even median = 2500.00
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  A (smaller)=[2000]  B=[1000,3000]  total=3 half=2
    │
    ▼
  binary search cut i in A; j = half - i
    │ i=0 j=2 : aL=-inf aR=2000 bL=3000 bR=+inf ; bL>aR → lo=1
    │ i=1 j=1 : aL=2000 aR=+inf bL=1000 bR=3000 ; cross OK
    ▼
  odd total → median = max(aL,bL) = max(2000,1000) = 2000
    ▼
  Output: median of combined order (no merge)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Median of Two Sorted Arrays finds the median of the combined order of two already-sorted arrays without merging them, and I solve it in logarithmic time in the size of the smaller array with constant space. The idea is a partition: I pick a cut in the smaller array, and the matching cut in the larger array is forced because the left side must hold exactly half the total elements, so knowing how many I took from one fixes how many come from the other.

I binary-search the cut in the smaller array and check a crossing condition: the largest element on the left of each array must not exceed the smallest element on the right of the other. If the left of the smaller array is too big, I move its cut left; if too small, I move it right. When both crossing conditions hold, I have the correct split, and for an odd total the median is the larger of the two left boundaries, while for an even total it is the average of the larger left boundary and the smaller right boundary.

The nuances I always mention are the edge sentinels and searching the smaller array. When a cut lands at the start or end of an array there is no element on one side, so I treat a missing left boundary as negative infinity and a missing right as positive infinity, which lets the crossing checks work uniformly. I always search the smaller array so the derived cut in the larger one never goes out of bounds and the complexity stays logarithmic in the smaller size. For money I compare and average with BigDecimal and a defined rounding mode.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to report the median transaction amount across Rajesh's and Priya's separately sorted amount lists without the cost of merging huge lists on every request. Explaining the partition idea, the crossing condition, the even-odd median formulas, and the infinity sentinels shows the interviewer that I understand one of the harder binary-search problems rather than just a merge shortcut.
